title: Workflows and agents: who owns the control flow?

items.stem: Your assistant's booking path is Python code with four steps: (1) a model call extracts machine, date and time from the student's message; (2) code calls check_calendar; (3) if the slot is free, code calls book_slot, otherwise code picks the next free slot; (4) a model call writes the confirmation. Which description fits best?

options.text: Agent: the model is called, and tools are used along the way
Workflow: the code picks every step, and the model fills in two of them
Agent: the path changes depending on whether the slot is free
Agent: the model words its extraction and confirmation differently each run

items.stem:
Here is the core of an assistant:

messages = [question]
for step in range(6):
    reply = model(messages, tools)
    if reply.tool_call is None:
        break
    messages.append(run_tool(reply.tool_call))

In one run the model requests check_calendar for Friday, then check_calendar for Saturday, then writes its answer. Who decided what in this run?

options.text: The code decided both calendar checks, because it executes run_tool each time
The model chose the checks, but the code chose when to stop, via the break
The model chose both checks and when to stop; the code only set the 6-step limit
The model chose Friday's check; the code chose Saturday's after seeing the result

items.stem: Every booking request goes through the same three steps: confirm the student's training record, check the calendar, book the slot. A booking must never be made without the training confirmation, and the model budget is small. Which design is best for this path?

options.text: Code runs the three steps in order, with one model call to write the reply
An agent with the three tools and a system prompt that requires the training check first
Code runs the training check, then an agent handles the calendar and booking
Code runs the steps, but a model call first decides whether this student needs a check

items.stem: Every model call costs $0.01. A fixed workflow always makes 3 model calls per request. An agent version makes between 2 and 8 model calls per request, and its loop has a hard cap of 8. Over 500 requests, how much more can the agent cost than the workflow in the worst case, in US dollars?

The team splits the assistant in two: booking is code that runs fixed steps, and manual search is a loop in which the model requests page lookups, capped at 6. Some questions need 1 lookup and some need 6, depending on what each page returns. For the manual-search part, who owns the control flow, and what does that mean for cost?

options.text: The code owns it, because the cap is in the code, so every request costs the same
The model owns it, so cost has no upper bound because loops cannot be capped
The code owns it, because the booking half is fixed, so the whole assistant is a workflow
The model owns it, so cost varies per request and is bounded only by the cap

items.stem: Three requests reach the assistant. A: "Book the laser cutter tomorrow at 3 pm." B: "What bed temperature do I use for PLA on the Prusa?" C: "Find any machine here that can cut 6 mm acrylic and book the earliest free slot this week." Only one of these is poorly served by a fixed workflow. Which one? Answer with the letter.
